title: Dense credentials take quadratic time: every re2-wasm exec copies the whole view (256 KiB of ghp_ tokens: 72 s)
body:
## Summary

Sanitizing text with many credential matches takes quadratic time in 0.12.1. Each `RE2#exec` call of re2-wasm copies the whole scanned view into WASM again, and gitleaks rules call `exec` once per match.

- 128 KiB of `ghp_` tokens takes about 18 s.
- 256 KiB takes 72 s, about 3.6 KB/s.
- Plain log text of the same size takes about 1 s.

#47 sped up ordinary large logs. This case is separate: it scales with the number of matches.

## Reproduction

`@link-foundation/sensitive-data-sanitizer` 0.12.1, Node.js 22, Linux x64. Each test file is newline-separated random `ghp_` + 36 alphanumerics, sanitized with `redact - --credentials-only --allow-binary` (with or without `--stream`, same result):

| Input                                         | Time        |
| --------------------------------------------- | ----------- |
| 32 KiB of tokens                              | 2.1 s       |
| 64 KiB of tokens                              | 5.4–6.0 s   |
| 128 KiB of tokens                             | 17.7–19.3 s |
| 256 KiB of tokens (one line, space-separated) | 72.5 s      |
| 64 KiB of git SHAs / base64 / UUIDs           | about 1.0 s |
| 300 KB of ordinary log lines                  | 1.7 s       |

Each doubling of the input roughly triples or quadruples the time. Line breaks don't matter: 128 KiB with one token per line takes 18.6 s.

Script: [experiments/issue-253/sanitizer-findings.sh](https://github.com/link-foundation/start/blob/issue-253-480126f69838/experiments/issue-253/sanitizer-findings.sh)

## Cause

`node --cpu-prof` on the 64 KiB input shows the time going to `exec` in `src/re2.js`, called from `ruleMatches` in `src/gitleaks.js:157`:

```
1666 ms  wasm-function[72]   exec@src/re2.js < ruleMatches@src/gitleaks.js:157 < scanRule < detectGitleaks
 519 ms  stringToUTF8Array   toWireType < exec@src/re2.js < ruleMatches ...
 334 ms  lengthBytesUTF8     toWireType < exec@src/re2.js < ruleMatches ...
```

`ruleMatches` loops `pattern.exec(text)` with `lastIndex`. Every call converts the full `text` to UTF-8 and copies it into the WASM heap (`toWireType`), then searches from `lastIndex`. With N matches in a view of L bytes, that is O(N·L) work for each rule that matches.

## Suggested fix

Any of these would make it linear:

- Run the RE2JS path that `large` views already use (no copy into WASM) once a view has produced more than a few matches.
- Or scan bounded windows around each rule keyword hit (gitleaks rules carry `keywords`) instead of the whole view.
- Or copy the view into WASM once and search it with offsets, if re2-wasm can be driven that way.

Please add a throughput test with a dense-token input, for example 256 KiB of `ghp_` tokens under a few seconds.
acceptance: closed upstream; independent regression audit required

title: Authorization tokens end at "]" or "}" and swallow a following NUL: "Bearer [REDACTED]" becomes "[REDACTED]]"
body:
## Summary

In 0.12.1 the token of an `Authorization: <scheme> <token>` header ends at the first `]` or `}`, and it does not end at a NUL byte. As a result:

- Sanitizing an already sanitized log is not idempotent: `Bearer [REDACTED]` becomes `[REDACTED]]`.
- Template placeholders leave their closing brackets behind: `Bearer {{token}}` becomes `[REDACTED]}}`.
- With `--allow-binary`, a NUL right after the token is masked along with it, so the output no longer keeps every non-secret byte.

Found while moving start-command to 0.12.1, which dropped its own Authorization pre-pass now that #45 is fixed (link-foundation/start#253). start sanitizes terminal transcripts, and those often hold logs that were already sanitized.

## Reproduction

`@link-foundation/sensitive-data-sanitizer` 0.12.1, Node.js 22, run with `redact - --credentials-only --allow-binary`:

| Input                                      | Output                                | Expected                                                                |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Authorization: Bearer [REDACTED] already` | `Authorization: [REDACTED]] already`  | `Authorization: Bearer [REDACTED] already` (or `[REDACTED] already`)    |
| `Authorization: Bearer {{token}} x`        | `Authorization: [REDACTED]}} x`       | `Authorization: [REDACTED] x` (or the placeholder kept, like `<token>`) |
| `Authorization: Bearer <token> x`          | `Authorization: [REDACTED] <token> x` | (consistent, for comparison)                                            |
| `Authorization: Bearer abc\0 tail`         | `Authorization: [REDACTED] tail`      | `Authorization: [REDACTED]\0 tail`                                      |

```sh
printf 'Authorization: Bearer [REDACTED] already\n' | sensitive-data-sanitizer redact - --credentials-only
printf 'Authorization: Bearer abc\0 tail\n' | sensitive-data-sanitizer redact - --credentials-only --allow-binary | od -c
```

A NUL after a non-Authorization credential is kept (`ghp_…\0` becomes `[REDACTED]\0`), so only the Authorization path is affected.

Script: [experiments/issue-253/sanitizer-findings.sh](https://github.com/link-foundation/start/blob/issue-253-480126f69838/experiments/issue-253/sanitizer-findings.sh)

## Cause

`authorizationRange` in `src/context.js`:

```js
if (text.startsWith(REDACTED, start)) {
  return undefined;
}
const match = /^(?:[a-z][a-z0-9_-]*[ \t]+)?[^\s"'\\,<>}\]]+/i.exec(
  text.slice(start)
);
```

- The `REDACTED` guard runs only before the scheme, so `Bearer [REDACTED]` slips past it. The token class then stops at `]` and masks `[REDACTED`.
- `}` and `]` end the token even when the token itself opened the bracket (`{{token}}`, `[REDACTED]`).
- `\0` and other C0 control bytes are not in the excluded class, so they become part of the token.

## Suggested fix

- Also skip, or keep unchanged, a token that starts with `[REDACTED]` after the scheme.
- When a token starts with `{`, `[` or `<`, end it at the matching closing bracket, or treat it as a placeholder the way `<token>` already is. Do not cut it at the first closing bracket.
- Add `\0` (`\x00-\x1f`) to the excluded class.
- Add the four rows above to the test suite.
acceptance: closed upstream; independent regression audit required

title: Large logs: file mode stops at the 60 s worker deadline (ERR_WORKER), one NUL byte blocks the log (ERR_BINARY), ~1 MB/s
body:
Large and real-world logs are blocked or slow with 0.12.0 `redact --stream --credentials-only`.

1. **File mode stops at the 60 s worker deadline.** `redact <file> --stream --output <out>` uses `sanitizeFileBounded` with `workerTimeoutMs ?? 60000` (`src/stream.js:397`), and the CLI has no option to change it. An 80 MB synthetic log fails after 61 s with `ERR_WORKER`. Stdin mode (`redact - --stream --output <out> < file`) completes the same file in 208 s, which is about 0.4 MB/s for this log (it has one 15 MB escaped-JSON line). Callers that need to finish have to use stdin mode.
2. **One NUL byte blocks the whole log** with `ERR_BINARY` (`src/stream.js:248`):
   ```
   $ printf 'line one\n\0line two\n' | sensitive-data-sanitizer redact - --credentials-only --stream --output out.log
   Sanitization failed; output was blocked (ERR_BINARY).
   ```
   Terminal transcripts sometimes contain NUL bytes. Failing closed is safe, but an opt-in such as `--allow-binary`, which treats NUL as an ordinary byte, would let these logs be published.
3. **Throughput.** Ordinary log text runs at about 1 MB/s, and CLI startup takes about 4 s. A 100 MB execution log therefore takes minutes.

Reproduction script: https://github.com/link-foundation/start/blob/issue-251-cce19f18f1c5/experiments/issue-251/upstream-repro.sh (with `make-large-log.js` next to it).

Output from `LARGE_MIB=80 experiments/issue-251/upstream-repro.sh`:
```
Sanitization failed; output was blocked (ERR_WORKER).
file mode exit=2 seconds=61
stdin mode exit=0 seconds=208
```
acceptance: closed upstream; independent regression audit required

title: --env-secrets masks configuration values of AUTH-named variables (GIT_AUTH_TRANSPORT=github.com masks every github.com)
body:
`--env-secrets` takes the value of every variable whose name matches `src/known.js` `secretEnvName`, including `AUTH` as a name part. Some of those values are configuration, not secrets, and masking them removes ordinary log content everywhere. Version 0.12.0:

```
$ printf 'git remote: https://github.com/owner/repo\n' |
  env GIT_AUTH_TRANSPORT=github.com sensitive-data-sanitizer redact - --credentials-only --env-secrets
git remote: https://[REDACTED]/owner/repo
```

A real case is the hive-mind host, which sets `HIVE_MIND_GIT_AUTH_TRANSPORT=github.com`. Every `github.com` in an uploaded log is masked there.

Possible fixes:
- skip values that look like host names, URLs, paths, booleans or short words;
- require a minimum length or entropy for literal env values;
- add an exclusion list for names such as `*_AUTH_TRANSPORT`, `*_AUTH_MODE` and `*_AUTH_METHOD` (similar to the `auth_mode` values in #40).

start-command used the same name rule before it moved to this library (link-foundation/start#250). The behavior is not new, but it now lives in one place.
acceptance: closed upstream; independent regression audit required

title: Authorization header values that are not double-quoted are masked to the end of the line
body:
`Authorization` header values that are not double-quoted are masked to the end of the line, so the rest of the line is lost. Version 0.12.0, `redact - --credentials-only`:

```
$ printf '%s\n' \
  'curl -H "Authorization: token ghx1234567890abcdefXYZ" keep-after' \
  "curl -H 'Authorization: token ghx1234567890abcdefXYZ' keep-after" \
  'Authorization: Bearer abc.def.ghi keep-after' |
  sensitive-data-sanitizer redact - --credentials-only
curl -H "Authorization: [REDACTED]" keep-after
curl -H 'Authorization: [REDACTED]
Authorization: [REDACTED]
```

`inspect()` shows which rules match:

```
"curl -H 'Authorization: token ghx1234567890abcdefXYZ' keep-after"
    context "token ghx1234567890abcdefXYZ' keep-after"
    gitleaks/curl-auth-header "ghx1234567890abcdefXYZ"
"Authorization: Bearer abc.def.ghi keep-after"
    context "Bearer abc.def.ghi keep-after"
    authorization "abc.def.ghi keep-after"
```

- `src/detection.js:191` `/(?:Proxy-)?Authorization[ \t]*:[ \t]*(?:Bearer|Basic|Digest)[ \t]+([^\r\n"',]+)/gi` does not stop at whitespace.
- The `context` rule (`src/context.js`, key `authorization`) takes everything up to the end of the line after a single quote or no quote at all.

This matters for logs that contain a long single-line JSON request body, where a header can appear inside a prompt. That is the case in link-foundation/start#249, where 2.9 MB of a 4.5 MB log was dropped. Expected: mask the scheme and one token, stopping at whitespace, a quote, `\` or `,`, as the double-quoted case already does.

start-command keeps a small pre-pass for now (`js/src/lib/log-sanitizer.js`, `AuthorizationHeaderMask`). It masks `Authorization: <scheme> <token>` before calling the CLI, and can be removed once this is fixed.
acceptance: closed upstream; independent regression audit required

title: Become the one sanitizer for gh-upload-log, start-command and hive-mind: publish to npm, and take over their practices (environment secrets, gh hosts.yml, non-UTF-8 bytes, unbounded lines, credentials-only mode)
body:
The maintainer wants one sanitizer for all our tools: link-foundation/gh-upload-log, link-foundation/start (`$ --upload-log`) and link-assistant/hive-mind should all use this library, and this library should take the best practices of all three. Today none of them depends on it, and each has its own rules.

Compared on 2026-10-23 (this repository 02104ac, start-command 0.39.1 main, hive-mind 2.39.6 main, gh-upload-log 0.12.1 main):

1. **Publish to npm.** `npm view @link-foundation/sensitive-data-sanitizer` returns E404, and there are no GitHub releases (#23, #28 were closed). The three tools cannot depend on it until it is published.
2. **Secret values from the environment, without listing names by hand.**
   - start-command masks the exact value of every environment variable whose name matches `/(?:^|_)(?:TOKEN|(?:API|ACCESS|PRIVATE)?KEY|SECRET|PASSWORD|PASSWD|CREDENTIALS?|AUTH|PAT)(?:_|$)/i`.
   - hive-mind keeps a curated list of AI-tool variables (`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`, `CODEX_API_KEY`, `OPENCODE_API_KEY`, `DASHSCOPE_API_KEY`, `HF_TOKEN`, `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN`, …, `src/token-sanitization.lib.mjs` `KNOWN_LOCAL_TOKEN_ENV_VARS`).
   - Here, `knownSecretsFromEnv` reads only explicitly named variables. Test: `MY_SERVICE_TOKEN=<value>` in the environment, and the same value in the input is kept.
3. **Local credential files.** hive-mind also reads GitHub tokens from `~/.config/gh/hosts.yml`, not only from `gh auth token`.
4. **Bytes that are not UTF-8** are kept by start-command (Latin-1 mapping), while this library blocks the whole output: see the encoding part of #41.
5. **Unbounded lines.** start-command streams in 64 KB blocks and keeps a continuation state, so a token or header longer than a block cannot leak its tail. hive-mind holds back up to 8 MB (`DEFAULT_MAX_HOLD_BYTES`). Here `--max-record-bytes` is 1 MB for text, and longer lines are slow (#41).
6. **Keep public account details.** For our logs, the maintainer: "Account details is public, not a leak." and "github.com/konard is public account." A tool should be able to run credentials-only (no personal-data replacement), or keep every EMAIL and account-ID finding of a stated list, without one `publicEntities` entry per value and a review date each.
7. **The false positives already fixed elsewhere**, see #40: hive-mind's npm package-name exemption (link-assistant/hive-mind#2156) and token-count exemption (link-assistant/hive-mind#2119; already correct here).

gh-upload-log has no sanitizer at all today, so for it this library would be the first one.


The moves are tracked in link-foundation/gh-upload-log#55, link-foundation/start#250 and link-assistant/hive-mind#3740.
acceptance: closed upstream; independent regression audit required

title: Long log lines are slow (runs of one character are quadratic: 100 KB 28 s, 1.5 MB > 9 min; base64 ~20 s/MB) and invalid UTF-8 blocks the whole output
body:
Logs from AI tools have very long single lines: escaped JSON request bodies (100 KB and more), and Codex rollouts with base64 images (one line is 3.6 MB on average and up to 15.7 MB). Measured with commit 02104ac, `redact --native-only --output`, on a MacBook:

| Input (one line) | Size | Time |
|---|---|---|
| `A` repeated | 25 KB | 1.95 s |
| `A` repeated | 50 KB | 7.17 s |
| `A` repeated | 100 KB | 28.24 s |
| `A` repeated | 1.5 MB | stopped after 9 min of CPU |
| random base64 in JSON | 100 KB | 1.33 s |
| random base64 in JSON | 1 MB | 19.72 s |
| base64 with zero-filled runs (like a PNG) | 1 MB | 12.05 s |
| 120,000 ordinary log lines, `--stream` | 14 MB | 7.24 s |

Time grows quadratically with the length of a run of one character, and about 20 s per MB for base64 lines. Base64 PNG data has long `AAAA…` runs wherever the image has flat areas.

Reproduce: `python3 -c "print('A'*100000)" > l.log; time node bin/sensitive-data-sanitizer.js redact l.log --native-only --output l.out`

Invalid UTF-8 also blocks the whole output:

```
printf 'ok line\n\xff\xfe invalid utf8 \xc3\x28 here\nsecond\n' > bad.log
node bin/sensitive-data-sanitizer.js redact bad.log --native-only
Sanitization failed; output was blocked (ERR_ENCODING).
```

Terminal logs often contain such bytes (binary output, cut multibyte characters). Blocking means the log is never published. start-command's sanitizer maps bytes through Latin-1 and keeps them (`src/lib/log-sanitizer.js`, "Latin-1 provides a reversible byte mapping, including invalid UTF-8").

Expected: linear time on long lines, so a 15 MB line finishes in seconds; invalid bytes are kept as they are (or replaced in a lossless way) while the valid text around them is still sanitized.
acceptance: closed upstream; independent regression audit required

title: False positives in tool logs: `sk-` inside words (`disk-baseline-…`), loopback and private IPs, `auth_mode`/`auth_method` values and shell expressions, package names, GitHub Actions `id-token`/`${{ secrets.X }}`
body:
Found while checking which sanitizer to use for hive-mind, start-command and gh-upload-log logs. Commit 02104ac (0.11.31), `redact --native-only` and default, same result. All inputs below are synthetic.

```
Command: gate='/tmp/hive-mind-disk-baseline-0ce9e170-e6d3-494d-91e1-0d820245d34b'
🧠 Formal AI: endpoint http://172.18.0.2:8080/api/openai/v1
proxy example: "socks5://127.0.0.1:1080"
INFO codex_otel.log_only: event.name="codex.conversation_starts" auth_mode="Chatgpt"
auth_method: "oauth"
use: curl -L -H "Authorization: token $(gh auth token)" -o <filename> <url>
  "devDependencies": { "secretlint": "^9.0.0", "next-auth": "^5.0.0", "@secretlint/secretlint-rule-preset-recommend": "^9.0.0" }
permissions:
  id-token: write
  token: ${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}
```

Output:

```
Command: gate='/tmp/hive-mind-di[REDACTED]'
🧠 Formal AI: endpoint http://[REDACTED]:8080/api/openai/v1
proxy example: "socks5://[REDACTED]:1080"
INFO codex_otel.log_only: event.name="codex.conversation_starts" auth_mode="[REDACTED]"
auth_method: "[REDACTED]"
use: curl -L -H "Authorization: [REDACTED]" -o <filename> <url>
  "devDependencies": { "secretlint": "[REDACTED]", "next-auth": "[REDACTED]", "[REDACTED]/secretlint-rule-preset-recommend": "[REDACTED]" }
permissions:
  id-token: [REDACTED]
  token: [REDACTED]
```

None of these values is a secret.

1. `openai` rule, `src/rules.js:14`: `/sk-(?:proj-|svcacct-|admin-)?[A-Za-z0-9_-]{16,}/g` has no left boundary, so it matches inside `disk-baseline-<uuid>` (every hive-mind execution log has this line). start-command has the same bug: link-foundation/start#249.
2. `ipv4`: loopback `127.0.0.1` and private `172.18.0.2`, `10.0.0.5`, `192.168.1.10` are redacted as personal data, while `8.8.8.8` is kept. Loopback, RFC 1918 and Docker bridge addresses identify no one.
3. `context` (SECRET): a value under an `auth*` key is masked even when it is a mode or method name (`Chatgpt`, `oauth`, `ApiKey`) or a shell expression (`$(gh auth token)`), which is the hive-mind system prompt text.
4. Package manifests: dependency names containing `secret` / `auth` and their version ranges are masked. hive-mind already exempts them (link-assistant/hive-mind#2156).
5. GitHub Actions: `id-token: write` is a permission, and `${{ secrets.X }}` is a reference, not a value. Reported for hive-mind in link-assistant/hive-mind#2841.

Expected: all lines above are unchanged, and regression tests cover them. The real credential cases keep working, for example `Authorization: token 0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567` is redacted, which this library already does correctly (hive-mind currently does not).
acceptance: closed upstream; independent regression audit required

title: After #37: 782/911 real sessions publish; remaining 129 blocked by SECRET/context label spans (prose 'token for', JSON keys after 'sig:')
body:
## Summary

Re-verification of #36 after PR #37 (`main` @ `edb778f`). All #36 reproductions and the `tel:` / `Fax:` leak are fixed. On the same real public-repository sessions, **782 of 911** now publish, up from 418:

| Result | After #35 | After #37 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| OK | 418 | **782** |
| `ERR_RESIDUAL` | 369 | 124 |
| `ERR_JSON_COLLISION` | 42 | 5 |
| `ERR_JSON` / `ERR_ENCODING` / `ERR_LATE_PERSONAL` / `ERR_FINDING` | 82 | **0** |

By source: Codex 672 of 765, Claude Code 110 of 146. Options: `{ structured: 'jsonl', profile: 'publication', twoPass: true, workers: 1 }`.

An independent leak audit of the 782 passing outputs found no leaks. It checked MRZ (with check digits), RU passport, SNILS and INN (checksums), PNR, ticket, visa, DOB, card (Luhn), IBAN, phone, `tel:`, email, IPv4, provider tokens, JWT, private keys, URL credentials and home paths. All remaining hits were false positives in the audit itself (UUID fragments, `noreply@github.com`, `/Users/runner/`, `{api_key}` placeholders).

The 129 remaining failures fail closed. Nothing leaks, but those sessions cannot be published. In every minimized case the cause is the **`SECRET/context` credential-label rule**, which has the same flaw #34 fixed for personal labels: a `token` / `sig` / `key` label word in prose captures text after it across escaped newlines, or captures JSON keys.

## Reproductions

Each one was minimized automatically from a real failing session, and none contains private data. Each fails in `sanitize`, `sanitizeJsonl` and `sanitizeStreamToFile` (one-pass and two-pass):

```js
sanitize(text, { profile: 'publication', structured: 'jsonl' });
```

### 1. `ERR_JSON_COLLISION`: `sig:` captures following JSON keys

```jsonl
{"payload":{"content":[{"text":"sig:' "},{"type":"","text":""}]}}
```

`SECRET/context` reports `sig:' `, then `type` and `text`, which are **object keys** of the next array element. Redacted: `{"[REDACTED]":"","[REDACTED]":""}`.

### 2. `ERR_RESIDUAL`: prose after `token for` / `SIG for` across `\n`

```jsonl
{"toolUseResult":{"stdout":"token for ES.\nes u"}}
{"toolUseResult":{"stdout":"SIG for\n:sig is d"}}
{"payload":{"content":[{"text":"token for\\ery record. The enclosing request-log write lock serio\\n/// this c"}]}}
```

Findings and redacted output:
- `"u"` → `token for ES[REDACTED]\nes u`. The redaction lands on `.`, and verification then finds `u` again.
- `"sig is d"` and `"d"` → `:sig is [REDACTED]`. Verification finds `sig is [REDACTED]` as a new secret.
- `"-log write lock serio"` → only `c` is redacted, and verification finds the same span again.

In all three, the span that detection reports differs from the span that redaction replaces (raw vs. decoded offsets), so verification sees the "secret" again. The values are ordinary English words, so they should not be detected at all. `token for`, `SIG for` and `sig is` are prose, not `key: value` assignments.

### 3. `ERR_RESIDUAL`: nested escaped quotes in a key assignment

```jsonl
{"payload":{"content":[{"text":"APIkey=\"\\\"private_key:9\""}]}}
```

`SECRET/context` reports both `\\\"private_key:9` and `9`. Redaction then throws `ERR_RESIDUAL`, presumably because the outer and inner findings overlap across escape layers.

## Expected

- Credential labels in prose (`token for`, `sig is`, `SIG for`) are not assignments. A `SECRET/context` value must follow `:` or `=` directly on the same logical line, must stop at escaped `\n` or a closing quote (as #35 did for personal labels), and must never include JSON keys or structural characters.
- When `structured` is set, the detection and redaction spans for `SECRET/context` use the same encoding layer, so verification cannot find the same span again.
- If a value is still detected after redaction, it is redacted again (fixed-point), not reported as a hard failure, as long as the output stays valid JSON.
- Add these record shapes to the publication corpus.

Related: #34, #36, #37. npm publication is still tracked in #28: `npm view sensitive-data-sanitizer` still returns 404.
acceptance: closed upstream; independent regression audit required

title: Real sessions still blocked after #35: name/state labels confirm code tokens and propagation rewrites raw JSON; twoPass still throws ERR_LATE_PERSONAL
body: ## Summary Re-verification of #34 after PR #35 (`main` @ `ada53fd`). The #34 reproductions are fixed, and the Codex Guardian prompt no longer crashes. Real sessions are still mostly blocked, though: **418 of 911** public-repository session files (≤ 5 MB) publish. Claude Code sessions are hit hardest, with only **9 of 146** passing. Every failure is fail-closed, so nothing leaked. The main root cause is the `name` / `state` catalog labels confirming arbitrary code tokens as personal values. Propagation then rewrites those tokens everywhere in the **raw JSON text**: JSON literals, keys and structural characters. Options used for every run: ```js await sanitizeStreamToFile(createReadStream(file), out, { structured: 'jsonl', profile: 'publication', twoPass: true, workers: 1, }); ``` | Result | Files (after #33) | Files (after #35) | | --- | ---: | ---: | | OK | 20 | **418** | | `SyntaxError` (raw) | 818 | 0 | | `ERR_RESIDUAL` | 49 | **369** | | `ERR_JSON_COLLISION` | 18 | 42 | | `ERR_ENCODING` | 2 | 36 | | `ERR_JSON` | 0 | 32 | | `ERR_LATE_PERSONAL` (with `twoPass: true`) | 6 | 10 | | `ERR_FINDING` | 0 | 4 | By source: Codex 409 of 765 OK, Claude Code 9 of 146 OK. (Two files from the earlier 913 were deleted locally in between. Three `ERR_OUTPUT` results were my harness reusing an existing target path; those files pass.) Throughput is much better: 129 MB of passing sessions took about 5,000 worker-seconds (about 0.026 MB/s per worker), and most files finish in seconds. Every reproduction below was minimized automatically from a real failing session, keeping only records and characters that are needed. None of them contains private data. Each one fails on its own as a JSONL file: ```js import { sanitize } from 'sensitive-data-sanitizer'; sanitize(text, { profile: 'publication', structured: 'jsonl' }); // and/or sanitizeStreamToFile(Readable.from([text]), out, { structured: 'jsonl', profile: 'publication', twoPass: true }) ``` ## 1. `name:` / `name=` confirms any following token as a person, then propagation rewrites raw JSON `PERSON/catalog/aws` and `PERSON/label` accept whatever follows `name:` or `name=`, including `null`, `codec`, `Coding`, `Claude`, `...`, `name` and `:{`. `document-propagation` then replaces every occurrence of that value in the raw JSONL text, outside string values as well. ### 1a. `ERR_JSON`: the JSON literal `null` is rewritten ```jsonl {"payload":{"collaboration_mode":{"settings":{"developer_instructions":null}}}} {"payload":{"content":[{"text":"name:null"}]}} ``` Redacted text: `"developer_instructions":[REDACTED]}`, which is invalid JSON. Every Codex `turn_context` record contains `null` literals, so any later `name:null` blocks the whole session. ### 1b. `ERR_JSON`: structural characters are rewritten (`nom:` label) ```jsonl {"payload":{"content":[{"text":"nom::{\\n"}]}} ``` `nom:` (Rust parser combinator crate, `nom::{...}`) is read as a name label with value `:{`. Redacted text: `{"payload"[REDACTED]"content":...`. ### 1c. `ERR_JSON_COLLISION`: key `limit_name` collides after propagating `name` ```jsonl {"payload":{"rate_limits":{"limit_id":"","limit_name":null}}} {"payload":{"content":[{"text":"name=name"},{"text":"id\"name:\"C"}]}} ``` This is the standard Codex `rate_limits` record shape. Fails in stream mode (two-pass: `ERR_JSON_COLLISION`; one-pass: `ERR_RESIDUAL`). ### 1d. `ERR_RESIDUAL`: propagated code tokens leave `::`, which the IPv6 rule then flags ```jsonl {"payload":{"content":[{"text":"name=codec"}]}} {"payload":{"content":[{"text":"codec::"}]}} ``` ```jsonl {"payload":{"content":[{"text":"ai\"name:\"Coding"},{"text":"a::coding_"}]}} ``` After redaction: `[REDACTED]::` and `a::[REDACTED]_`, which give a residual `IP_ADDRESS/ipv6` on `::` and `a::`. Rust paths (`codec::`, `serde_json::`, `a::b`) are everywhere in coding sessions, so `::` and `x::` must not count as IPv6 addresses. ### 1e. `ERR_RESIDUAL`: Claude Code tool schemas (`name:Claude`) ```jsonl {"attachment":{"tools":[{"schema":{"input_schema":{"properties":{"capabilities":{"description":"name:Claude"}}}}},{"schema":{"description":"name:..."}}]}} {"rendered":[{"content":"Claude..."}]} ``` The product name `Claude` (and `...`) becomes a personal seed taken from a tool description. Fails in stream mode; the in-memory `sanitizeJsonl` passes. This is the main reason Claude Code sessions fail (9 of 146 pass). **Expected:** a `name` / `nom` label value must look like a person's name before it is confirmed. That excludes JSON or JS literals (`null`, `true`, `undefined`), punctuation-only values, the label word itself, product names and lowercase identifiers. Propagation and redaction must also act only inside JSON **string values** when `structured` is set, and never on keys, literals or structural characters. ## 2. `ERR_RESIDUAL`: `ENCODED_SENSITIVE` found but never redacted ```jsonl {"toolUseResult":{"stdout":"\"Elon Musk"}} ``` `inspect` reports `ENCODED_SENSITIVE/encoded` (0.85) on `\"Elon Musk`, but redaction leaves it unchanged. Verification finds the same finding again and fails. This is a public figure, so it should probably be preserved. Either way, detection and redaction disagree. ## 3. `ERR_ENCODING` on an escaped cookie header ```jsonl {"payload":{"content":[{"text":"\"cookie:;\\n\""}]}} ``` `SECRET/cookie` matches across the escaped quote and `\\n`, and redaction throws `ERR_ENCODING`. (`sanitizeJsonl` passes; `sanitize`/stream fail.) This blocked 36 Codex sessions with `curl -H "Cookie: ..."` style commands. ## 4. `ERR_FINDING` from `inspect` on an `Authorization:` header ```jsonl {"wireToolInputs":{"toolu_01EXAMPLE":{"command":"Authorization:\""}}} {"toolUseResult":{"stderr":""}} ``` `inspect` itself throws `ERR_FINDING`, which suggests an internal finding with an invalid span when the credential label sits at the end of a JSON string. This is the Claude Code `wireToolInputs` record shape. ## 5. `ERR_LATE_PERSONAL` even with `twoPass: true` 10 files still fail with `ERR_LATE_PERSONAL` under `twoPass: true`. Instrumenting `streamIdentity.confirm()` on one of them shows two problems: 1. Pass 1 registers the value with a trailing space: ``` .[0].status,result:.[0].conclusion,count:length})),failures:(.statuscheckrollup|map(select(.conclusion == ``` Pass 2 confirms the same value **without** the trailing space and as a `STATE/known-personal` finding, so `values.has(normalized)` misses and pass 2 throws `ERR_LATE_PERSONAL`. Pass 1 and pass 2 must produce the same seed for the same text, for example by trimming before normalizing, or by matching pass-2 `known-personal` findings against the registry instead of re-seeding from them. 2. The value comes from a public `gh pr view --json statusCheckRollup --jq '{...map({state:.[0].status,...})...}'` command. `STATE/catalog/azure` reads the jq object key `state:` as a US-state / location label. This part reproduces synthetically: ```js inspect(JSON.stringify({ text: `gh pr view 1 --json statusCheckRollup --jq '{counts:(.statusCheckRollup|map({state:.[0].status,result:.[0].conclusion,count:length}))}'` }), { profile: 'publication', structured: 'json' }); // → STATE/catalog/azure on ".[0].status,result:.[0].conclusion,count:length}))..." ``` The same run also registered `==` and `check` as personal values. I could not reproduce the pass-1/pass-2 mismatch synthetically in a small file: it needs about 70 records of the real session. The instrumented output above is the evidence. A unit test where pass 2 gets a `known-personal` finding whose span differs from the registered value only in surrounding whitespace should cover it. **Expected:** under `twoPass: true`, pass 2 must never throw `ERR_LATE_PERSONAL`, because every value is known after pass 1. If pass 2 still finds something new, it should redact it, not fail. ## 6. Leak (minor): `tel:` links without `+` and `Fax:` labels are not detected This one was found by an independent audit of the 418 **passing** outputs. A fetched public organization web page kept its phone numbers, while the email on the same page was redacted: ```js sanitize(JSON.stringify({ text: 'Fax: 028 12 345 678' }), { profile: 'publication', structured: 'json' }) // unchanged sanitize(JSON.stringify({ text: 'ĐT' }), ...) // unchanged sanitize(JSON.stringify({ text: 'tel:+84812345678' }), ...) // tel:[REDACTED] (OK) sanitize(JSON.stringify({ text: 'Phone: 028 12 345 678' }), ...) // Phone: [REDACTED] (OK) ``` **Expected:** a `tel:` URI is always a phone number (with or without `+`), and `Fax:` / `ĐT` (Vietnamese "điện thoại") should be phone labels. The rest of the audit found no MRZ, passport, SNILS, INN, PNR, DOB, email, card, token or home-path leaks in the passing outputs. ## Acceptance - The reproductions in 1–4 and 6 publish with valid JSON and zero residual findings, keep `null` / keys / structure untouched, and keep code tokens (`codec::`, `nom::{`, `Claude`). - `twoPass: true` never throws `ERR_LATE_PERSONAL`. - Add Codex `turn_context` / `rate_limits` records and Claude Code `attachment.tools` / `wireToolInputs` / `toolUseResult` record shapes to the CI publication corpus from #35. Related: #34, #35. npm publication remains tracked in #28 (package is still 404 on npm).
acceptance: closed upstream; independent regression audit required

title: Real sessions still blocked after #33: label spans across escaped JSON newlines crash propagation, JSON keys read as names, CI paths as users
body:
## Summary

Re-verification after #33 (main @ c60b9e1) with `profile: publication` and `structured: jsonl`. The probes and minimal reproductions from #18 to #31 now pass: 34/34 identity probes, bare passport, SNILS and INN masked, `userName = getUserName()` untouched, and the #30 snippets stay valid JSON. However, real sessions still cannot be published:

- documents-processing (13 files): 12 fail (`ERR_RESIDUAL`, `ERR_OUTPUT`, `ERR_JSON_COLLISION`).
- public repositories, all session files up to 5 MB, partial run: of the first 62, 40 crash with `SyntaxError`, 2 fail with `ERR_ENCODING`, and 20 pass.
- a 23 MB public Codex session: `ERR_RESIDUAL` with `workers: 1`, `ERR_LATE_PERSONAL` with `workers: 4`.

The library fails closed, so nothing leaks, but almost nothing can be published.

## 1. Label value spans the rest of a JSON string, then propagation crashes (`SyntaxError: Stack overflow`)

Inside a JSON string, line breaks are escaped `\n`. A `phone`/`email` label value therefore runs to the end of the string, up to a whole 937-line file. Propagation then compiles that value into a RegExp. The error is not an `ERR_*` failure: streaming reports it as `ERR_OUTPUT` and `sanitizeJsonl` throws a raw `SyntaxError`.

```js
const s = createSanitizer({ profile: 'publication' });
const body = (n) => Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => `  const value${i} = compute(${i});`).join('
');
const src = (n) => `function parse(line, found, number) {
  if (relation) {
    found.emergencyRelationship ??= relation;
  } else {
    found.phone = number;
  }
${body(n)}
}`;
await s.sanitize(src(5));                                   // "found.phone = [REDACTED]"  (code identifier as a phone)
await s.sanitize(JSON.stringify({ content: src(5) }));      // 314 chars -> 24 chars: whole file content replaced (PHONE:label 165 chars)
await s.sanitize(JSON.stringify({ content: src(900) }));    // throws SyntaxError: Invalid regular expression ... Stack overflow
```

Expected: label values stop at escaped line breaks and quotes, and have a bounded length. A phone or email value must look like one, not like code (`number;`). Propagation escapes and bounds seeds, never compiles values above a small limit, and turns every internal exception into an `ERR_*` failure.

## 2. JSON keys are treated as names (regression from #26), then key collisions block records

```js
const p = createSanitizer({ profile: 'publication' });
await p.sanitize('root_turn_id');                          // "[REDACTED]_id"  PERSON:name-document
const j = createSanitizer({ structured: 'jsonl', profile: 'publication' });
await j.sanitizeJsonl('{"payload":{"root_turn_id":"x","other_turn_id":"y"}}
'); // ERR_JSON_COLLISION
```

Codex session records contain `turn_id` and `root_turn_id`. Expected: the document-file-name rule requires a real file name (an extension or a path) and gazetteer or name-shaped words, not `snake_case` identifiers. Structured mode never rewrites JSON keys that are ordinary identifiers.

## 3. CI logs: GitHub Actions paths treated as personal

```text
node:internal/test_runner/test:835:12             -> node:internal/test_[REDACTED]/test:835:12
location: '/home/runner/work/example-repo/...'   -> location: '[REDACTED]'
# Subtest: passes the standalone validator used by the filing workflow -> passes [REDACTED]
/home/runner/work/_temp/...   /github/runner_temp/... -> /home/[REDACTED]/...  /github/[REDACTED]_temp/...
```

`runner` (and `ubuntu`, `vsts`, `circleci`, `node`, `root`) are well-known service accounts, not personal user names. Propagating them into `test_runner` and `runner_temp` is wrong.

The same public CI output also triggers `ERR_RESIDUAL` in structured mode. Line-level minimisation does not shrink it, because the failure needs the propagation state built by several lines. The record below is public GitHub Actions output from link-foundation/relative-meta-logic.

## 4. `ERR_LATE_PERSONAL` blocks streams with parallel workers

The same 23 MB public session fails with `ERR_LATE_PERSONAL` with `workers: 4`. Please add a two-pass mode to `sanitizeStreamToFile`, and to the CLI: pass 1 collects confirmed personal values, pass 2 redacts with the complete registry. Late confirmations then never block an atomic file publication.

## 5. `ERR_ENCODING` on session files

2 of the first 62 public session files fail with `ERR_ENCODING`. Session logs can contain lone surrogates escaped in JSON (`\ud83d`) or invalid bytes from tool output. Please handle escaped lone surrogates in structured mode, and report the record and offset in the failure.

## 6. Throughput and npm

- Throughput could not be measured on real sessions because of the failures above; the files that pass ran at about 0.02 to 0.1 MB/s per worker.
- npm: still 404. #28 says owner setup is required; tracked there.

## Acceptance

A CI job runs `sanitizeStreamToFile(..., { structured: 'jsonl', profile: 'publication' })` over a corpus of real-shaped Claude Code and Codex sessions: tool results with source code, CI logs, Codex `turn_id`/`root_turn_id` records, and emoji and surrogate escapes. It requires zero failures and zero residual findings.

comments.body:
## Final numbers: all public-repository session files up to 5 MB (913 files), main @ c60b9e1

`sanitizeStream(source, { structured: 'jsonl', profile: 'publication', workers: 1 })`:

| Result | Files |
| --- | ---: |
| OK | 20 |
| `SyntaxError` (raw, not `ERR_*`) | 818 |
| `ERR_RESIDUAL` | 49 |
| `ERR_JSON_COLLISION` | 18 |
| `ERR_LATE_PERSONAL` | 6 |
| `ERR_ENCODING` | 2 |

Passing files ran at about 0.02 MB/s per worker.

## Why 818 crash: the standard Codex system prompt

Every Codex session embeds the Guardian prompt, which contains `- Organization: default generic organization / personal user.`. The `Organization:` label value runs across escaped `\n` to the end of the JSON string. It is also matched as `ORGANIZATION:catalog/azure`. Propagation then compiles it into a RegExp:

```js
const p = createSanitizer({ profile: 'publication' });
const tail = (n) => Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => `- Rule ${i}: apply this policy to the current planned action (${i}).`).join('\n');
const text = (n) => `# Security Policy\n## Environment Profile\n- Organization: default generic organization / personal user.\n${tail(n)}`;
await p.sanitize(JSON.stringify({ text: text(3) }));    // 80 chars left: the whole prompt is replaced (ORGANIZATION:label 237 chars)
await p.sanitize(JSON.stringify({ text: text(400) }));  // SyntaxError: Invalid regular expression: /default[ \t_-]+generic[ \t_-]+o...
await p.sanitize(text(400));                            // raw text works: the bug is specific to escaped JSON newlines
```

This one fix (label values stop at escaped line breaks, and propagation seeds are bounded and escaped) should unblock most sessions. The vendor system prompts of Claude Code and Codex should be part of the regression corpus, since every session contains them.

acceptance: closed upstream; independent regression audit required

title: Over-redaction: inconsistent public figures, uppercase words as booking refs, implausible fake phones
body:
## Summary

These are over-redaction and quality problems found while re-checking #15–#23 on main @ c9714cb. None of them leak data, but they damage published sessions and conflict with #1 (public people should not be treated as personal data) and #5 (ordinary uppercase words after "booking" are negatives).

### 1. Public figures handled inconsistently

| Input | Result |
|---|---|
| `Linus Torvalds`, `Elon Musk tweeted`, `Bill Gates`, `Nelson Mandela`, `Satya Nadella`, `Tim Cook`, `Grace Hopper` | kept |
| `Sergey Brin founded Google` | `[REDACTED] founded Google` |
| `Pavel Durov said` | `[REDACTED] said` |
| `Vladimir Putin` | `[REDACTED]` |

The result appears to depend on whether the first name is in the (Slavic) gazetteer, not on whether the person is public. Expected: the bundled public-entity catalog (or `createWikidataVerifier`) takes precedence over the gazetteer for well-known public figures regardless of the name's origin. Add these as fixtures.

### 2. Uppercase words and places taken as identifiers or names

| Input | Result |
|---|---|
| `Booking FAILED today` | `Booking [REDACTED] today` (`BOOKING_REFERENCE`) |
| `reservation HTTP 500` | `reservation [REDACTED] 500` |
| `Marina Bay Sands hotel` | `[REDACTED] Sands hotel` (`PERSON`) |

Expected: booking references must contain at least one digit or match a PNR shape that is not a dictionary word. Add negatives for common uppercase log words (`FAILED`, `ERROR`, `HTTP`, `PENDING`, `OK`, `CANCELLED`, `CONFIRMED`). A first name directly followed by a known place/brand word (`Bay`, `Sands`, `Hotel`, `Street`) should not become a person on its own.

### 3. Fake mode: phones not in a plausible or reserved range (#22)

`mode: 'fake'` turns `phone +7 912 555-01-42` into `+7 227 479-47-38`. The country code and length are kept, but `227` is not a Russian mobile range, and #22 asked to prefer reserved fictional ranges where available. Expected: keep the number type (mobile stays `9xx` for RU) and use reserved/fictional ranges where they exist (NANP 555-01xx, Ofcom drama ranges, …).

The faked MRZ, dates, SNILS, names and emails were verified to be valid, deterministic per key and different across keys. Credentials stay fully redacted.

title: Regression from #15: bare formatted SNILS and 12-digit INN no longer redacted (required by #11)
body:
## Summary

The fix for #15 (bare checksum matches get confidence 0.35 and are not replaced under the default `minConfidence: 0.5`) also turned off detection that #11 explicitly required. #11: "Russian SNILS (`ddd-ddd-ddd dd` with checksum) and INN (10/12 digits with checksum) without labels. With a `snils`/`inn` label both are detected; bare values such as `112-233-445 95` are not."

On main @ c9714cb:

| Input (synthetic, checksum-valid) | Result |
|---|---|
| `СНИЛС 112-233-445 95`, `snils 11223344595` | redacted ✅ |
| `112-233-445 95` | **unchanged** (`RU_SNILS` 0.35) |
| `пенсионное 112-233-445 95` (common Russian name of SNILS) | **unchanged** (0.35) |
| `value 500100732259` (12-digit personal INN) | **unchanged** (`RU_INN` 0.35) |

Plain 10-digit numbers matching INN/NHS/NPI checksums by chance are a different case from the SNILS shape. `ddd-ddd-ddd dd` with exactly that punctuation and a valid checksum almost never appears by accident in logs: it is strong structural evidence on its own, like a formatted credit card number. A 12-digit INN with two check digits passes by chance only about 1 in 100 times, unlike the 1-in-10 10-digit INN.

## Expected

- SNILS in its formatted shape `ddd-ddd-ddd dd` (and `ddd ddd ddd dd`) with a valid checksum scores ≥ 0.85 without context.
- 12-digit INN (two check digits) scores above the default threshold, or at least above it whenever any Russian-language text is in the same record. 10-digit INN stays low without context, as #15 requires.
- Add SNILS context words: `пенсионное`, `страховое свидетельство`, `СНИЛС`, `страховой номер`.
- Add a test asserting the confidence for each national-ID shape, so a future threshold change cannot silently disable a required detector. List the effective default behaviour per ID type in COVERAGE.md.
acceptance: closed upstream; independent regression audit required

title: Names still leak after #20: file names with non-gazetteer names, Slavic name pairs in prose, propagation across stream batches
body:
## Summary

#20 is closed, but personal names still leak in the same forms that caused the original incident. Detection depends on the first name being in the gazetteer. Names next to document words in file names are found only when both parts are known gazetteer entries. Document-level propagation does not cross streaming batches, which is the only way to process the large sessions where the leak happened.

All values below are synthetic. Tested on main @ c9714cb with `createSanitizer({})`.

### 1. File names with document words (explicitly required by #20)

| Input | Result |
|---|---|
| `KOVALEVA_MARINA_PASSPORT.jpg`, `IVANOV_IVAN_SCAN.pdf`, `KUZNETSOVA-EKATERINA-ID.png` | redacted ✅ |
| `SIDOROV_ALEKSEI_PHOTO.png` | **unchanged** |
| `SIDOROV-ALEKSEI-PHOTO.png` | **unchanged** |
| `TKACHENKO_BOGDAN_VISA.pdf` | **unchanged** |
| `ZHANG_WEI_PASSPORT.pdf` | **unchanged** (`Zhang Wei` in prose *is* redacted) |
| `NGUYEN_VAN_AN_PASSPORT.jpg` | **unchanged** |
| `scan_passport_kovaleva_marina.jpg` (lowercase, document word first) | **unchanged** |
| `ПАСПОРТ_Ковалева_Марина.pdf` (Cyrillic; `ПАСПОРТ` is listed in #20) | **unchanged** |

Expected: two or three name-shaped tokens joined by `_`/`-` next to a document word (PASSPORT, VISA, ID, PHOTO, SCAN, ПАСПОРТ, ВИЗА, СКАН, ФОТО), in either order and any case, are `PERSON` structurally. A gazetteer hit should only raise confidence, not be required.

### 2. Name pairs in prose (required by #20: "transliterated Slavic surnames -ova, -eva, -ov, -ev, -in, -ina, -enko, -sky")

| Input | Result |
|---|---|
| `Alexey Sidorov`, `Ekaterina Kuznetsova` | redacted ✅ |
| `for Olesya Zyryanova`, `Zyryanova Olesya` | **unchanged** |
| `Aleksei Sidorov` (common transliteration of the same name) | **unchanged** |
| `Bogdan Tkachenko` | **unchanged** |
| `Ковалева Марина`, `Зырянова Олеся` (Cyrillic, no patronymic, no label) | **unchanged** |

Expected: a capitalised (or all-caps) given-name-shaped token adjacent to a token with a Slavic surname suffix counts as a name pair. Transliteration variants of gazetteer names (`Aleksei/Alexei/Alexey/Aleksey`, `Olesya/Olesia`) must be covered systematically, for example through transliteration normalisation of the gazetteer instead of single spellings. Cyrillic surname-suffix + first-name pairs need the same rule.

### 3. Propagation stops at streaming batch boundaries

`sanitizeStream(src, {structured: 'jsonl'})` on a 1.7 MB JSONL: the first record holds a synthetic MRZ for `ZYRYANOVA<<OLESYA`, and the last record says `saved zyryanova_olesya_scan.png for Olesya Zyryanova`. **The last record is published unchanged.** The same text through `sanitize()` (one batch) is redacted. API.md documents "Document propagation is within a scanned batch", but streaming exists precisely for the large sessions where this leak happened (#23). Propagation also does not cross scripts: `ФИО: Зырянова Олеся` + `файл zyryanova.pdf` redacts only the Cyrillic name.

Expected:
- The stream keeps a bounded, private per-stream registry of confirmed personal values (from MRZ, labelled fields and strong rules) and applies it to all later batches. Because earlier batches are already emitted, a confirmed value seen only *after* its first occurrence must either be handled by a two-pass mode (`sanitizeStreamToFile` can scan twice) or make the stream fail closed.
- Confirmed Cyrillic names propagate in their standard transliterations (ICAO 9303 / GOST 7.79 / common passport spellings) and back.

### Tests

Add every input above as a regression fixture, plus a stream test where the confirmation and the reuse are more than one batch apart.
acceptance: closed upstream; independent regression audit required

title: Sanitization by faking: realistic same-format fake values (valid MRZ, dates, checksums, script-preserving names)
body:
## Summary

Add sanitization by faking: replace real values with realistic fake values of the same format, so published sessions stay readable and their code paths, tests and parsers still work. Today `format-preserving` produces character-class noise, and `pseudonym` produces opaque tags.

## Current behaviour (main @ 2306fda, synthetic input)

```text
format-preserving:
  P<RUSKOVALEVA<<MARINA<<<…  ->  Z<ZCRCEXHADTT<<ZDQAAR<<<…   (invalid document code, invalid state, letters only)
  5839204716RUS8204117M310519<<…  ->  7936874368RTY3267065H912481<<…  (invalid country RTY, sex H, impossible dates, wrong check digits)
  Ковалева Марина Сергеевна  ->  qprwhpqc geasxb jzdxreurb   (Cyrillic replaced with Latin noise)
  born on 07/12/1985  ->  born on 55/46/5121                 (impossible date)
  phone +7 912 555-01-42  ->  +5 585 882-10-71               (country code changed)
pseudonym:
  every value -> [PSEUDONYM_2856bd99eef0eebb9ecf79d4]
credentials: always [REDACTED] (no fake option)
```

## Proposal: `mode: 'fake'`

Keyed and deterministic, so the same input value always maps to the same fake within a run, and consistently across types:

- **Names:** fake names from the same locale and script and gender (Cyrillic stays Cyrillic, patronymic stays a patronymic). The same person is consistent between the MRZ, prose, labelled fields and file names.
- **Dates:** valid calendar dates, shifted by a keyed offset, with the original format kept (`dd/mm/yyyy`, ISO, `dd.mm.yyyy`). Birth dates stay plausible, for example adults stay adults.
- **Passport MRZ:** valid ICAO 9303 lines with real check digits. The issuing state and nationality are kept, or replaced by `UTO` (configurable). Name fields match the faked name, and date fields match the faked birth and expiry dates.
- **Document numbers and national IDs:** same length and pattern with valid checksums (SNILS, INN, PESEL, Luhn and others). Prefer reserved or specimen ranges where they exist.
- **Phones:** keep the country code and number length. Use reserved fictional ranges where available, such as NANP 555-01xx and Ofcom drama numbers.
- **Emails and domains:** fake local parts on reserved domains (`example.com`, `.test`).
- **Credentials (opt-in):** a provider-shaped fake that cannot be valid and carries a visible marker, for example `ghp_FAKE…`. It must not trip GitHub push protection or other scanners, and full redaction stays the default for credentials.
- Every fake is recognisable by the residual verifier (`kept: 'fake'` / `faked: true` findings), so verification does not loop on its own output. The `fakeIdentity` policy also recognises fakes produced by this mode.
- Document that faked output is a pseudonymisation, not anonymisation: the key must stay private, and structure such as dates and relations is partly preserved.

## Tests

Round-trip properties: generated MRZ lines pass check-digit validation. Dates parse. Checksummed IDs validate. Scripts are preserved. The same input maps to the same output under one key and to different output under another key. No original value survives.
acceptance: closed upstream; independent regression audit required

title: identityMask/fakeValues: label findings include label words ("no***YZ") and ignore allowlisted values
body:
## Summary

With `identityMask: true`, a generic `ID:label` finding claims a span that includes the label words, so the mask shows label text instead of the value. `fakeValues` is ignored for the same reason.

## Reproduction

```js
const s = createSanitizer({ identityMask: true, fakeValues: ['AB1234XYZ'] });
await s.sanitize('passport no AB1234XYZ');      // => "passport no***YZ"   (expected "passport no AB1234XYZ", allowlisted)
await s.sanitize('passport number: AB1234XYZ'); // => "passport nu***YZ"   (label text leaks into the mask)
await s.sanitize('passport no 7549302813');     // => "passport no***13"   (expected "passport no 75***13")
// findings: ID:label spans start at "no" / "number: ", not at the value
```

## Expected

- Label findings start at the value, not at trailing label words like `no`, `no.`, `number:`, `#` or `№`.
- Passport context produces `PASSPORT_NUMBER`, not the generic `ID`, so identity policies apply uniformly.
- `fakeValues` matching uses the value span, and also a whole token when a detector span is a substring of it.
- Short values: `pnr: AB12` is not detected at all. Decide whether 4-character values after booking or passport context should be fully redacted, as the identity policy suggests.

```js
const s = createSanitizer();
for (const t of [
  "This trip's affected flights are on Air India booking K7QWZP",
  "out: 'AirIndia-K7QWZP-2-AI0000-AAA-BBB-cancelled.pdf'",
  "const SUPPORT_DIR = path.join(FINAL, 'K7QWZP');",
]) console.log((await s.sanitize(t)).text);
// K7QWZP survives in all three
```

## Expected

- `booking`, `reservation`, `PNR`, `confirmation` and `бронь` alone, followed by a 5–8 character uppercase alphanumeric token, count as booking context. This includes airline names in between ("Air India booking K7QWZP").
- A value confirmed as a booking reference anywhere in the same input is redacted at every occurrence, including inside file names and path segments. This is a document-level propagation of confirmed values, which would also help passport numbers and names.
- Airline-prefixed file names `<Airline>-<PNR>-...` count as booking context.
acceptance: closed upstream; independent regression audit required

title: ERR_RESIDUAL blocks real sessions and the visa rule redacts words without digits
body:
## Summary

After #14, real AI session files are blocked with `ERR_RESIDUAL`. It fails closed, which is safe, but those sessions can never be published. The minimal reproduction contains no personal data. A second bug shows up alongside it: the new visa rule redacts ordinary words that contain no digits.

## Reproduction (main @ 2306fda)

```js
const s = createSanitizer();
await s.sanitize('{"stdout":"nameis\\nvisawindo"}');   // throws ERR_RESIDUAL
await s.sanitize('name is\nvisa window');              // => "name is\nvisa [REDACTED]"
await s.sanitize('nameis visawindo');                  // => "nameis [REDACTED]"
```

The same happens with `structured: 'jsonl'` + `sanitizeJsonl()`. Two of the ten Codex session files tested (about 5 MB each) failed this way. The trigger was ordinary code-review prose containing the word "visa" in an escaped JSON string.

## Expected

- `VISA_NUMBER` requires at least one digit, and a shape of an actual visa or e-visa identifier, not any word after "visa".
- The escaped-JSON projection and the residual verification agree on spans, so no `ERR_RESIDUAL` occurs when the first pass already redacted everything the second pass sees.
- Regression tests: the snippets above, plus prose like "the visa window closes", "visa application form", "Visa card".
acceptance: closed upstream; independent regression audit required

title: Remaining gaps from #8 and #12: MRZ fake check per document, ID/TH phone formats, label words in identity spans
body:
## Summary

Two acceptance cases from #8 and #12 still fail on main @ 2306fda. A third (span precision) is minor.

### 1. Fake identity: descending document number is redacted when the MRZ name line is present (#8)

With `fakeIdentity: 'specimen-and-synthetic'`:

| Input (synthetic) | Result |
|---|---|
| `9876543217RUS9001014F300101<<<<<<<<<<<<<<04` alone | kept, 2 findings `kept: 'fake'` ✅ |
| `P<RUSTESTOVA<<OLGA<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<` + `\n` + the same line | **whole MRZ `[REDACTED]`, 0 kept** ❌ |
| German specimen `Reisepass C01X00T47 MUSTERMANN ERIKA SPECIMEN` | **`Reisepass [REDACTED]`** ❌ (#8 lists `MUSTERMANN`/`SPECIMEN` as national specimen markers; `C01X00T47` is the published German specimen number) |
| ICAO TD1/TD3 `UTO`/`ERIKSSON` specimens | kept ✅ |

Expected: the fake decision is made per document (the MRZ as a unit, using its document-number field) and applies to all lines of that MRZ. Add the specimen document numbers of common national documents (DE `C01X00T47` / `T22000129`, etc.) and recognize `MUSTERMANN`/`ОБРАЗЕЦ`/`SPECIMEN` when they are part of the same document record. Context words like "test" must still not exempt anything.

### 2. National trunk formats for Indonesia/Thailand only work after messenger labels (#12)

| Input (synthetic) | Result |
|---|---|
| `WhatsApp: 0812 3456 7890` | redacted ✅ |
| `0812 3456 7890` | unchanged ❌ |
| `telp 0812-3456-7890` (Indonesian "phone") | unchanged ❌ |
| `HP: 0812 3456 7890` (Indonesian "mobile") | unchanged ❌ |
| `โทร 08 123 4567` (Thai "call") | unchanged ❌ |
| `gọi 090 123 4567` (Vietnamese "call") | redacted, but as `UK_NHS` (wrong type) |

#12 asked for these trunk formats as format rules, plus local call-to-action context. Expected: add local phone/call vocabulary for at least the languages in #12 (`telp`, `telepon`, `HP`, `hubungi`, `โทร`, `เบอร์`, `gọi`, `SĐT`, `điện thoại`) and the trunk-prefix shapes (with space, dash and parentheses), typed `PHONE`.

### 3. Minor: label words are swallowed into identity spans

`passport no J8369854`, `passport number J8369854`, `passport No. J8369854` all become `passport [REDACTED]`. With `identityMask: true`, `passport no J8369854` becomes `passport no***54`: the kept "first two characters" are the label word `no`, not the value. Expected `passport no J8***54` (#7's 2+2 rule applies to the value). The `ID:label` span should start after `no`/`number`/`No.`/`№`/`#`.

Similarly, prose password context now runs to the end of the line. `password=hunter2 email john@private.org then more text` becomes `password=[REDACTED]`, which hides the unrelated rest of the line. That is safe but over-broad. For `key=value` syntax, the value should stop at whitespace, while prose forms (`password is …`) keep the wider span.
acceptance: closed upstream; independent regression audit required

title: 'author' matches as credential label and 'Date:' headers are redacted (git log, HTTP, email)
body:
## Summary

Two context rules fire on very common log fields that are not sensitive:

1. **`author` is treated as a credential label.** The `auth` key affix matches `author`, `authored_by` and `"author":`. Every `git log`/`git show` output, `package.json`, and commit metadata in an AI session gets `SECRET:context` (0.95 VERY_LIKELY).
2. **`Date:` headers are redacted as `DATE` (`catalog/azure` rule).** Git log dates, HTTP `Date:` response headers and email headers are removed. #6 explicitly required: "Keep plain dates (commit dates, timestamps) untouched without birth context."

## Reproduction (main @ 2306fda, `createSanitizer({})`)

| Input | Output | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| `author=octocat` | `author=[REDACTED]` | `SECRET:context` 0.95 |
| `"author": "Some Name"` | `"author": "[REDACTED]"` | `SECRET:context` |
| `authored_by: bot` | `authored_by: [REDACTED]` | `SECRET:context` |
| `commit 1a2b3c4\nAuthor: github-actions[bot] <…noreply…>` | `Author: [REDACTED] <…>` | `SECRET:context` |
| `Date:   Wed Oct 7 12:00:00 2026 +0300` (git log) | `Date:   [REDACTED]` | `DATE:catalog/azure` 0.95 |
| `Date: Wed, 07 Oct 2026 12:00:00 GMT` (HTTP) | `Date: [REDACTED]` | `DATE:catalog/azure` |
| `Date: 2026-10-07` | `Date: [REDACTED]` | `DATE:catalog/azure` |

`created: 2026-10-07T12:00:00Z` is correctly kept. So the issue is the `Date` label in the Azure catalog rule, not date parsing.

## Expected

- Credential key affixes must match on word boundaries: `auth`, `auth_token`, `x-auth`, `authorization` yes; `author`, `authored`, `authority`, `authorize_url` no. Add negatives for each.
- A person's name after `Author:` may still be `PERSON` through the name rules (and `Jane Roe` already is). It must not be a credential.
- A generic `DATE` (catalog) finding must not redact by itself. Only `DATE_OF_BIRTH` (or other dates with personal context) should redact by default, as #6 specified. Add git-log, HTTP-header and email-header fixtures as negatives.
acceptance: closed upstream; independent regression audit required

title: False positives: bare timestamps and order ids redacted as INN/NHS/NPI/credit card with VERY_LIKELY confidence
body:
## Summary

Since PR #14, the default engine redacts ordinary numbers in logs that have no identity context. Bare checksum rules (`RU_INN`, `UK_NHS`, `US_HEALTHCARE_NPI`) and the Luhn card rule fire on Unix timestamps, millisecond timestamps and order ids. They also report them as `VERY_LIKELY`. AI session logs and CI logs contain these numbers on almost every line, so a large part of the output is destroyed. In non-structured mode, a JSON number also becomes the string marker, so `{"timestamp":[REDACTED]}` is no longer valid JSON.

This conflicts with #11, which asked for "Presidio-style confidence tiers (low without context, high with context or checksum)", and with #4, which asked for "numbers next to unrelated digits (timestamps, version numbers, phone numbers) to keep false positives measured".

## Reproduction (main @ 2306fda, `createSanitizer({})`)

| Input | Output | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| `ts=1696023757` | `ts=[REDACTED]` | `US_HEALTHCARE_NPI:entity-format` 0.85 LIKELY |
| `ts=1696087109` | `ts=[REDACTED]` | `RU_INN:national-format` **0.99 VERY_LIKELY** |
| `ts=1696110866` | `ts=[REDACTED]` | `UK_NHS:national-format` **0.99 VERY_LIKELY** |
| `{"timestamp":1696023757}` | `{"timestamp":[REDACTED]}` (invalid JSON) | NPI |
| `elapsed 1696000628374` | `elapsed [REDACTED]` | `CREDIT_CARD:luhn` (13 digits starting with `1`; no card network uses that prefix) |
| `order 1015032381` | `order [REDACTED]` | `RU_INN` |
| `gọi 090 123 4567` (Vietnamese phone) | redacted, but typed as `UK_NHS` | wrong type |

Measured on 400 generated values each (no identity context anywhere):

| Shape | Redacted |
|---|---|
| `ts=<10-digit Unix seconds>` | 105/400 (26%) |
| `order <10 digits>` | 96/400 (24%) |
| `elapsed <13-digit ms timestamp>` | 37/400 (9%) |
| `run <13 digits>` | 34/400 |
| `id <11 digits>` | 14/400 |

These rates match chance: one check digit passes about 1 in 10 random numbers, and mod-11 about 1 in 11.

## Expected

1. Checksum-only matches without context get low confidence (≈0.3–0.4, `UNLIKELY`/`POSSIBLE`), as in Presidio. A context word in a window (`ИНН`, `NHS`, `NPI`, `SNILS`, `patient`, …) raises it to high.
2. A `minConfidence` / `threshold` option, defaulting to a value that does not redact bare low-confidence checksum matches. A strict publication preset can still lower it explicitly.
3. Credit cards require a valid IIN/network prefix and length (Visa 4 / 13,16,19; Mastercard 51–55, 2221–2720; Amex 34/37 / 15; Discover, JCB, UnionPay, Mir 2200–2204, …), not Luhn alone.
4. Numbers in known timestamp contexts (`timestamp`, `ts`, `time`, `created_at`, `elapsed`, `duration`, `ms`, epoch range 2000–2100) are negatives.
5. Phone numbers that also pass NHS mod-11 are typed `PHONE` when phone context or a trunk prefix is present.
6. Add a regression corpus of realistic log/session lines (timestamps, ids, sizes, ports, PIDs, line:col) with a measured false-positive rate checked in CI.
acceptance: closed upstream; independent regression audit required

title: Detect national-format phone numbers after messenger labels (WhatsApp, Zalo) and in Russian prose
body:
## Summary

National-format phone numbers without a `+` country code are missed after messenger labels and in Russian prose. A real publication of sanitized sessions exposed about 10 contact numbers from scraped rental advertisements this way. The Telegram handle on the same line was redacted, but the WhatsApp and Zalo numbers next to it were not.

## Reproduction (synthetic numbers)

```js
const s = createSanitizer();
for (const t of [
  'Telegram: @rent_agent_x | WhatsApp: 8 912 555 0142\nZalo: 090 123 4567',
  'Сергей, звоните 8 912 555 0142',
]) console.log((await s.sanitize(t)).text);
// => Telegram: [REDACTED] | WhatsApp: 8 912 555 0142\nZalo: 090 123 4567
// => Сергей, звоните 8 912 555 0142
```

By contrast, `WhatsApp: +7 912 555-01-42`, `Zalo: +84 90 123 4567` and `тел. 8 (912) 555-01-42` are detected.

## Expected

- Messenger labels (WhatsApp, Zalo, Viber, Telegram, Signal, WeChat, LINE, KakaoTalk) count as phone context, also when several `label: value` pairs share one line separated by `|`.
- National trunk-prefix formats: Russia `8 9xx xxx xxxx`, Vietnam `0[35789]x xxx xxxx`, Thailand `0x xxx xxxx`, Indonesia `08xx xxxx xxxx`, with space, dash and parenthesis grouping.
- Russian imperative call-to-action context (звоните, пишите, звонить, номер телефона) as context words.
- Negatives: tool-call ids such as `call_<digits>…`, thread ids in test output, and timestamps.
acceptance: closed upstream; independent regression audit required

title: National identifiers without short labels: NHS, RRN, codice fiscale, NRIC, PESEL, personnummer, SA ID, TFN, SIN, SNILS, INN
body:
## Summary

National identifiers that competitors test are only reachable through long catalog names, not through common short labels or format rules. All probes used synthetic values.

- UK NHS number (10 digits with mod-11 check) without a label.
- Korean RRN, Italian codice fiscale, Singapore NRIC/FIN, Polish PESEL, Swedish personnummer with common short labels (`RRN`, `CF`, `NRIC`, `PESEL`, `personnummer`).
- South African ID (13 digits with Luhn).
- Australian TFN and Canadian SIN short labels (`TFN`, `SIN`).
- Russian SNILS (`ddd-ddd-ddd dd` with checksum) and INN (10/12 digits with checksum) without labels. With a `snils`/`inn` label both are detected; bare values such as `112-233-445 95` are not.

## Expected

Format rules with checksum validation where public algorithms exist, Presidio-style confidence tiers (low without context, high with context or checksum), and fixtures per country.
acceptance: closed upstream; independent regression audit required

title: Missing credential formats found in competitor test suites: .netrc, NuGet, WordPress keys/salts, PuTTY v3
body:
## Summary

A comparison against competitor test suites (noseyparker, gitleaks HEAD, trufflehog, detect-secrets, secretlint) found credential formats that are missed. All probes used synthetic values.

| Format | Example (synthetic) | Covered by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.netrc` credentials | `machine api.example.net login alice password Zq8vR2mT9xLp` | noseyparker `np.netrc.1` |
| NuGet API key | `oy2` + 43 lowercase alphanumerics | noseyparker `np.nuget.1` (gitleaks rule is limited to `nuget.config` paths) |
| WordPress keys and salts in `define()` | `define('AUTH_KEY', 'q8Zv#R2m!T9xLp@Q7nWc4bY6dF1hJ0kS');`, also `SECURE_AUTH_KEY`, `LOGGED_IN_KEY`, `NONCE_KEY`, `*_SALT` (`DB_PASSWORD` is already detected) | noseyparker, ggshield |
| PuTTY v3 private key | a complete `PuTTY-User-Key-File-3:` block including `Private-Lines` and `Private-MAC` is returned unchanged | gitleaks matches only `File-2` |

## Expected

The `.netrc` triplet is missed both on one line and across lines. Detect each format with complete-span redaction, plus negatives for placeholders (`password ${PASS}`, `define('DB_PASSWORD', '')`, `example.com`). The vendored gitleaks rule set is current (222 rules at HEAD), so these need native rules.
acceptance: closed upstream; independent regression audit required

title: Session JSONL sanitization fails with ERR_LIMIT and redacts JSON structure (tool names, ids)
body:
## Summary

Sanitizing AI session logs (Claude Code / Codex JSONL) with the documented APIs is not practical today:

1. `sanitize()` / `sanitizeStream()` / the `redact --stream` CLI fail with `ERR_LIMIT` on ordinary records. The encoded-run scanner throws when a percent-encoded run or a wrapped base64 block exceeds 8192 characters, and session logs contain long URLs and base64 tool outputs.
2. On JSON text the engine redacts structural values: tool names (`"name":"Read"` as `PERSON`), message/request/tool-call ids (`toolu_…`, `req_…`, `msg_…` as `SECRET`), and whole skill descriptions as `SECRET context`. This makes the output useless for conversion tools that rely on these fields.

## Reproduction (synthetic data)

```js
const s = createSanitizer();
await s.sanitize(JSON.stringify({ url: 'https://example.org/search?q=' + 'word%20'.repeat(2000) })); // throws ERR_LIMIT
await s.sanitize('A'.repeat(100) + ('\n' + 'B'.repeat(100)).repeat(120));                       // throws ERR_LIMIT
const r = await s.sanitize(JSON.stringify({ type: 'tool_use', id: 'toolu_01CM9SwFYXq3vJ6cjYAFFjkf', name: 'Read' }));
// => {"type":"tool_use","id":"[REDACTED]","name":"[REDACTED]"}
```

## Expected

- An over-long encoded run should not block the whole input. Decode it in bounded windows, or fall back to non-decoded detection for that run, and report it as a finding.
- A JSON/JSONL-aware mode, for example `sanitizeJsonl()` or `structured: 'json'`, that sanitizes string values and keys separately, keeps the document parseable, and lets callers declare structural fields (ids, tool names, types) as non-personal.
- Performance: the current engine processes about 0.1–0.4 MB/s, so a 750 MB session takes hours. Batching or worker parallelism inside the library would help.

Workaround used downstream: walk every JSON string value, batch values with a separator, and fall back to `decode: false` on `ERR_LIMIT`.
acceptance: closed upstream; independent regression audit required

title: Allow explicitly fake identity data (specimens, synthetic numbers, reviewed allowlist) but never by context words
body:
## Summary

Allow explicitly fake identity data, such as test fixtures and documentation specimens, while redacting everything else. Today a project cannot tell the sanitizer "this passport line is a known fake", so it has to choose between over-redacting test fixtures and leaking real data.

## Proposal

A value is treated as explicitly fake only when one of these holds:

1. It is an official specimen: ICAO Doc 9303 specimen data (issuing state `UTO`, `ERIKSSON<<ANNA<MARIA`, document numbers such as `L898902C3`), national specimen markers (`SPECIMEN`, `ОБРАЗЕЦ`, `MUSTERMANN`).
2. It is obviously synthetic: one repeated digit, or 6 or more consecutive ascending or descending digits in the document number (`123456`, `987654`).
3. It is listed in a reviewed allowlist supplied by the caller (`fakeValues: [...]`), which is kept outside the published data.

Context words like "test", "fake" or "example" next to the value must NOT be enough. In the real leak that prompted this issue, real passport data appeared inside tests and messages such as "real-data tests".

## Expected

- Option `fakeIdentity: 'specimen-and-synthetic'` (default off for credentials, recommended on for identity documents).
- Findings for kept fake values are reported with `kept: 'fake'`, so audits can count them.
- Residual verification ignores only values that pass the same fake check.

## Tests

ICAO specimen TD3 lines kept; `9876543217RUS9001014F300101...` kept (descending document number); a realistic synthetic number such as `5839204716RUS...` redacted even when the line says "test passport".
acceptance: closed upstream; independent regression audit required
